Density, however, is said because of the compactness of the parts, so that the passage of the sensible species is impeded, whether it is hard as a dry wall, or soft as a wall made of new, soft clay. And between all the rare and dense things, water is the medium, because it is somewhat dense, yet in a way it is pervious, and similarly other things in which much water abounds, such as wine and lees and urine and such like, just as glass, crystal, and such like, which are more dense in a sensible way than air, yet they are rare in comparison with the earth, because we see through them.

<margin>They lack four feet</margin> for they lack four feet: this makes them unjust: for they either carry little grass or, if they do, it is all pestilential, as I have previously stated: from this it is not difficult to collect: that the frequent transport of salt by men causes more work: when so much salt is poured onto that river, which is believed to be the Sea: each individual builds small hills from the salt: and they arrange them so that one follows the other continuously along the straight path: and one person marks a certain place with a stake: and then all leave by the middle of the day's journey. When they have arrived, others who are black come to meet them: who do not wish to be known: and they do not allow any conversation with others: and they approach with their own Liburnian ships:

<margin>Exchange of salt and gold</margin> from larger islands, which they call the islands and the coast: they offer a certain amount of gold for the salt: as the trade seems to agree: and not from equality of the goods: and then they leave the salt and the gold: the black men, who had completed their journey by the middle of the day, return again: and one person takes a certain amount of salt from another: and if the salt offered is pleasing, they take it and leave the salt: and they go away without returning. If, however, the condition of the left gold is not pleasing, then both parties abandon it: namely, the gold and the salt: and they go away again at the same time as before: the black men who do not wish to be known again approach and take the gold from those from whom they saw the gold being taken: or they add a little gold to those who still have some gold left: or, if they do not wish to add more, they carry the gold away: leaving the salt: and in this way they conduct their trade: so that one does not see the other with the old established method: although this might seem to be against faith, as it might not be believed: but this is accepted as a matter of honor, because it is received from those worthy of faith, especially from the traders.

For nature indeed, which at first was entirely good, has been entirely corrupted through sin, and thus has lost justice and immortality. Hence, it could produce only corrupt, unjust, and mortal children. And the devil rightly required children into servitude, whose freedom he had bought from their first parents. Just as they had once been all parents, so too they became all destroyers: and (which is most wretchedly) first destroyers, before they became parents. For if the first parents and their descendants had obeyed God's commandment and preserved the original gift of justice, they would have lived in great peace and tranquility. Because their reason (that is, the power to understand and know things that are to be done and knowable) could not have gone astray, if they had obeyed God and conformed themselves entirely to Him: the will would have obeyed reason, sensuality would have yielded to desire, and even brute animals would have been subject to the rule of man. With the original justice remaining, the body was bound inseparably to the soul. For men, free from cold, heat, thirst, hunger, sickness, and finally from all bodily and spiritual weariness, after a life well and blessedly lived, and after the performance of many good works, would have been translated without the penalty of death into heaven.

To this our Cœlitus, implore the air; implore the powerful power of the divine, that I may be able to bear what presses upon me, the weight, and the price, and bring back from the quest the salvation.

To the Three Envoys of the Council.

When the venerable fathers have entrusted you with the care of the vineyard, you must carry out the work properly. First, the most skillful should be employed, so that the vineyard may be properly tilled and that luxury is entirely removed from everywhere. Any weeds, whatever they may be, should be uprooted. The overgrown parts should be cleared and brought back into cultivation. The entire vineyard should be enclosed with a strong fence, so that neither poor animals nor wild beasts may enter. The fierce wild animals must be kept out, for they are dangerous. It is necessary to prevent the violent and savage beasts from acting according to their usual habits, so that they do not devour the vineyard. The wild beasts, driven by their fierce rage and fierce snarl, are accustomed to burst forth from the dark forest and enter the vineyard, often penetrating deep into it, and with their own kind, leading their fine goats, to corrupt all the vines with their poisoned teeth. This wild beast has caused no damage to any vineyard, and has left no trace of harm from its inhuman madness. It is not content with itself, nor with the goats, and when the wild beasts have free access and the vineyard is often broken into, it attacks it for plunder. You, who have the vineyard to adorn and cultivate, must take care to restrain this beast, so that it does not enter.

IN. XII. In the annals of the same Quadrigarius, at the beginning of the book, it is written thus. If for your goodness, and our will, health has been granted to you: this is what we hope for, that the gods will do good things. Also in Valerius Antias, book iv. and xx., it is written in a similar way. If these things are done by the gods, and rightly interpreted: the augurs said that everything will proceed according to the opinion. Plautus also in the Casina, when speaking about the girl: said, "I will kill you," with these words.  
"Does the Casina have a sword?" "Yes, but two, with one I will kill you, with the other a servant."  
Also Laberius in the Gemellis.  
"I did not think," he says, "that he would do this."  
Therefore, these men did not know what the so-called "solecism" would be.

It is notable that the original text should have the word "spring" replaced with "vapor"; then it adds that the whole surface of the earth was watered, that is, the central vapor had passed through all permeable parts. Why, then, was the earth first watered by the subterranean vapor, and not by the superterranean rain, and thus stimulated to its first fertility? We will deal with this later, when we discuss the fertility of the central vapor. But here, if we consider it, why some versions of Holy Scripture use the word "vapor" and others "spring," we can easily reconcile them; for when vapors cool, they resolve into water and springs, as all alchemical distillations testify. Nor does this imply that the earth was watered in its prime by a kind of original fertility through aqueous vapor in some places, and through springs or rivers flowing from them in others; for we still see this happening. Experience teaches us that aqueous vapors moisten the earth, and that the Nile is also watered by its overflow. Therefore, this passage of Holy Scripture is very helpful for our demonstration, both because it explicitly says that vapors came from the earth, of whose present existence the mountains are a clear sign, as Vitruvius testifies, although it should be taken with caution. For when the seas swell at night, distillations toward the center are also more abundant, and hence evaporation from the center is again stronger during the day.
